image.prompt:
A SEAMLESSLY TILING TOP-DOWN GROUND TEXTURE. This is a flat material swatch, not a photograph of a scene or of an object. The camera looks straight down at the ground from directly overhead, perfectly orthographic, with no perspective, no horizon, no vanishing point and no tilt.

The surface: Flat square of plain unmarked asphalt road surface seen as a single unbroken sheet, no lane markings, no kerb, no sidewalk, no drains and no covers, edge to edge asphalt only Materials: Seamlessly tiling patched grey-black asphalt matching the plain road tile in tone and aggregate, dark tar crack seams and rectangular pothole patches, chalky worn white paint thinned and scuffed where wheels cross it, faint tyre-polish lanes either side of the centre line, thin dust and oil spotting; the asphalt and the paint must both wrap on the two ends so a run of tiles gives one continuous unbroken dashed line with even gaps.

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.

COMPOSITED AFTERWARDS by scripts/tilekit/composite.mjs, in metres on the 8 m frame: the geometry above is deliberately absent from the generated surface.

notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The whole surface reads out of the texture; nothing is modelled. This is the marked variant of a DECOMPOSED road kit: the carriageway carries no sidewalk at all, and the sidewalk is a separate placeable strip (Concrete Sidewalk Strip, 2.0 m wide and 0.15 m tall). Splitting them is the entire point of this set -- a builder puts a sidewalk down one side, both sides or neither, and nothing inside the road texture has to line up with anything inside the sidewalk texture, which is the alignment problem this replaces. Its asphalt base must be the SAME tone, aggregate and grain as the Plain Asphalt Road Tile so the two interleave in one run without the join reading as a change of surface; that shared base is the reason the pair exists rather than one tile. The markings fix the geometry of the piece: the dashed centre line runs down the tile's centreline, and the two solid edge lines sit 0.6 m in from the two edges the centre line runs between, giving a 6.8 m two-lane carriageway inside an 8 m tile. Because the paint has a direction, this tile is only TWO-way rotationally symmetric -- it drops in at 0 or 180 degrees along the road, and a 90 degree rotation deliberately turns it into a crossing street. The dash cycle must divide 8 m evenly and wrap at both ends, or a run shows a short dash at every tile boundary; that is the first thing to check on the generated texture. The contract is otherwise the same as the rest of the set: 8 x 8 m footprint on the kit's 8 m grid, pivot base-center so tiles snap on 8 m centres, asphalt seamless on all four edges. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. Quality comes entirely from a high-end tiling PBR texture and not from mesh detail; that is the whole bet of this piece. Manhole covers and drain grates are deliberately NOT in this texture: they are separate small props dropped on top wherever wanted. No destruction groups: a road tile is static level geometry, not a breakable. Note for anyone mixing sets: the kit's older road-straight-tile bakes a 1.25 m flat sidewalk band into the road texture and is a different, incompatible family -- do not run it in the same street as this one. The rigid geometry on this tile is NOT generated: six seeds of the apron grid and one of the lane markings landed the pattern off the 8 m frame, breaking it at every boundary, so prompts.image asks the generator for the bare SURFACE only and scripts/tilekit/composite.mjs draws the geometry afterwards at known coordinates in metres. That is what makes the pitch divide 8 m and the lines wrap exactly, by construction rather than by luck, and it is the same split scripts/tilekit/substrates.mjs already uses for the road markings.
